focus.text: An adverb clause answers a question about the main clause: when did it happen, why did it happen, what was it for, and what stood in its way. It begins with a subordinator such as when, because, although or so that, and it can never stand alone, because it needs a main clause beside it. Put the adverb clause first and you give the reader the background before the point; put it second and the main idea comes first. English allows only one linking word for each relationship.

summaryTable.caption: Four jobs an adverb clause does
rows: Time
when, while, before, after, as soon as, until, since
**When the rain stopped**, we cycled home.
Reason
because, since, as
We left early **because the road floods easily**.
Contrast
although, even though, whereas, while
**Although the course is short**, it covers a lot.
Purpose
so that, in order that
She revises at night **so that the house is quiet**.

pretest.sentence: As soon as the bell rings, the canteen fills up.
pretest.reason: *As soon as* introduces a time clause, and a clause in front position takes a comma.

pretest.sentence: Although the ticket was cheap, but the seat was uncomfortable.
pretest.reason: *Although* already marks the contrast, so *but* must go.

pretest.sentence: Because the library closes at nine, so we finished our essays at home.
We recycle our bottles because the school gives points for it.
pretest.reason: A reason clause that follows the main clause needs no comma.

pretest.sentence: I could not join the trip. Because my brother was ill that weekend.
pretest.reason: A *because* clause cannot be a sentence on its own; attach it to the clause before.

pretest.sentence: While my parents were cooking, I finished my homework.
pretest.reason: *While* with the past progressive sets the longer background action.

pretest.sentence: When I will graduate, I will apply for a scholarship.
pretest.reason: A future time clause takes the present: *When I graduate*.

pretest.sentence: Having finished the survey, the team wrote up the results.
pretest.reason: A reduced clause is correct here because both halves share the subject *the team*.

pretest.sentence: While walking to school, the rain became much heavier.
pretest.reason: A reduced clause must share the subject of the main clause, but the rain was not walking.

pretest.sentence: The trip was cancelled, as the coastal road had been damaged.
pretest.reason: *as* can introduce a reason clause, and a comma helps when it follows the main clause.

context.title: The footbridge
context.paragraph: Before the new footbridge opened, students from our neighbourhood crossed the main road twice a day. Because the traffic was heavy, many parents walked with them until they reached the gate. The district council finally agreed to build the bridge so that children could cross safely. While the work was going on, the lessons started half an hour later. Although the bridge is narrow, it has changed the morning completely. Since it opened in March, no accident has been reported near the school. My younger brother now leaves home at seven, whereas he used to leave at half past six. When he comes back in the afternoon, he no longer looks frightened.
targets: so that children could cross safely
While the work was going on
whereas he used to leave at half past six
When he comes back in the afternoon

sections.title: Forming an adverb clause

table.caption: Where the adverb clause goes, and how it is punctuated
rows: Clause first
subordinator + subject + verb, then the main clause
**Because the fee rose**, fewer students enrolled.
Clause second
main clause, then subordinator + subject + verb
Fewer students enrolled **because the fee rose**.
Never on its own
the clause is not a sentence by itself
Incorrect: *Because the fee rose.*

notes: Use a comma when the adverb clause comes first. When it follows the main clause you usually need none, although a contrast clause with *whereas* or *while* reads better with one.
Every adverb clause has its own subject and verb. *Because of* is a preposition and takes a noun: *because of the rain*, but *because it was raining*.

items.stem: ___ the results came out, Mai had already applied to two universities.
items.reason: *Before* orders the two events; *until* would mean the applying stopped at that point.

items.stem: The match was postponed ___ the pitch was flooded.
items.reason: *because* introduces a clause with a subject and a verb; *because of* takes a noun.

items.stem: ___ the course was expensive, Hải still decided to take it.
items.reason: The second clause is a surprise, so the link is contrast, not reason.

items.stem: She left her phone at home ___ concentrate better.
items.reason: *in order to* takes the base verb; *so that* needs a subject and a verb after it.

items.stem: As soon as the results ___, I will call you.
items.reason: A future time clause takes the present, not *will*.

sections.title: Using time clauses

rules.text: Use *when*, *after* and *as soon as* for one event that follows another, and *while* or *as* for two things happening together.

examples.text: **As soon as the ferry docked**, the passengers hurried off.
bold: As soon as the ferry docked

examples.text: **While Nga was revising**, her brother was watching a match.

rules.text: Use *until* for the moment something stops, and *since* for the starting point of a period that reaches the present.

examples.text: The shop stays open **until the last customer leaves**.
Traffic has been worse **since the factory opened**.

rules.text: In a time clause about the future, use a present form, never *will*.

examples.text: **When I finish** my degree, I will look for work in Đà Nẵng.
We will start the meeting **after everyone arrives**.

tips: Time clauses give a paragraph its spine. In a Task 1 description, *before*, *after* and *until* show the reader exactly where a trend turned.

sections.title: Using reason, contrast and purpose clauses

rules.text: Use *because*, *since* or *as* for a reason. Choose *because* when the reason is new information for the reader.

examples.text: Many families cycle to work **because petrol has become expensive**.
**Since the hall was full**, the talk was moved outside.

rules.text: Use *although*, *even though* or *though* for a contrast, and *whereas* or *while* to set two different facts side by side.

examples.text: **Although the app is free**, very few students use it.
Hà Nội has four seasons, **whereas Cần Thơ has two**.

rules.text: Use *so that* with a subject and a modal for purpose. When the subject does not change, *in order to* plus the base verb is shorter.

examples.text: The council widened the pavement **so that pedestrians could pass safely**.
bold: so that pedestrians could pass safely

examples.text: I set two alarms **in order to catch the early bus**.
bold: in order to catch the early bus

rules.text: Never use two linking words for one relationship: *although* or *but*, and *because* or *so*.

examples.text: **Although the rent is high**, the flat is close to campus.
**Because the rent is high**, many students share a room.

notes: *Since* has two meanings: a starting point in time (*since 2020*) and a reason (*since you are already here*). The verb forms around it usually make the meaning clear.

sentences: The road was closed for repairs.
We took the long way round.
model: Because the road was closed for repairs, we took the long way round.
We took the long way round because the road was closed for repairs.
items.reason: One linking word is enough, so *so* is not added to the second clause.

model: The film had already started when we arrived at the cinema.
By the time we arrived at the cinema, the film had already started.
items.reason: The earlier of the two events takes the past perfect.

sentences: Thousands of people came to the festival.
model: Although the weather was cold, thousands of people came to the festival.
Thousands of people came to the festival even though the weather was cold.
items.reason: *Although* or *even though* carries the contrast on its own, with no *but*.

sentences: Lan takes notes on her phone.
She wants to revise on the bus.
model: Lan takes notes on her phone so that she can revise on the bus.
Lan takes notes on her phone in order to revise on the bus.
items.reason: *so that* is followed by a subject and a modal; *in order to* by the base verb.

sentences: Đà Lạt stays cool all year.
Huế becomes very hot in June.
model: Đà Lạt stays cool all year, whereas Huế becomes very hot in June.
While Đà Lạt stays cool all year, Huế becomes very hot in June.
items.reason: *whereas* and *while* compare two facts, so both clauses stay true.

sections.title: Reducing an adverb clause

table.caption: Full adverb clause to reduced clause
rows: **While she was waiting** for the bus, Mai read an article.
**Waiting** for the bus, Mai read an article.
drop the subject and *be*, keep the *-ing* form
**After he had sent** the form, Khoa felt relieved.
**Having sent** the form, Khoa felt relieved.
use *having* + past participle for the earlier action
**Although it was written** in 1990, the report is still useful.
**Although written** in 1990, the report is still useful.
keep the subordinator, drop the subject and *be*
**Because she was born** in Huế, Trang has a central accent.
**Born** in Huế, Trang has a central accent.
with *because*, the subordinator goes too

notes: You can only reduce an adverb clause when both halves have the same subject. *While I was cycling, the rain started* cannot be reduced, because the rain was not cycling.
A reduced reason clause keeps no subordinator, so the link is weaker. If the reason has to be obvious, keep *because* and the full clause.

items.sentence: Although the training was free, but only twelve people came.
items.reason: *Although* already marks the contrast, so *but* must go.

items.sentence: Because the deadline was moved, so we had an extra week to revise.
items.error: so we had an extra week

items.sentence: When the exam results will arrive, the school will post them online.
items.reason: A future time clause takes the present, not *will*.

items.sentence: I stayed in the library. Because my flatmates were having a party.
items.reason: A *because* clause is not a sentence, so it joins the main clause.

items.sentence: While walking home, my phone suddenly stopped working.
items.reason: A reduced clause must share the subject, and the phone was not walking.

sections.title: Using subordinators, transitions and prepositions

rules.text: A subordinator joins two clauses inside one sentence, a transition links two separate sentences, and a preposition takes a noun phrase. Keep the three apart.

examples.text: **Although the fee rose**, enrolment stayed the same.
The fee rose. **However**, enrolment stayed the same.
**Despite the higher fee**, enrolment stayed the same.

rules.text: Choose the subordinator that carries the exact meaning you want. *Even though* is stronger than *although*, and *as* is weaker than *because*.

examples.text: **Even though she had studied for months**, Nhung was nervous.
bold: Even though she had studied for months

examples.text: The trip was cancelled, **as the road had been damaged**.
bold: as the road had been damaged

rules.text: Put the idea the reader already knows in the front clause and the new idea in the main clause. This keeps a paragraph moving forward.

examples.text: **After the survey was published**, the council changed the timetable.
**Because the timetable changed**, buses now run every ten minutes.

tips: *Despite* and *in spite of* take a noun or an *-ing* form, never a clause: *despite the delay*, *despite arriving late*, but *although we arrived late*.

editing.text: Last September I started a part-time job in a bookshop near my university in Hà Nội. Although the pay was low, but I took it because the owner let me revise during quiet hours. Because the shop opened at eight, so I had to leave home before seven every day. While walking to the bus stop, my bag often felt twice as heavy. I kept the job for four months. Because I wanted to save money for a laptop. My manager, who she came from Huế, taught me how to order stock. Despite the shop was small, it sold more than a thousand titles. I left in January so that I can concentrate on my exams. When I will finish my degree, I would like to work in publishing again.

errors.reason: *Although* already marks the contrast, so *but* must go.

errors.span: While walking to the bus stop
errors.fix: While I was walking to the bus stop
errors.reason: A reduced clause must share the subject of the main clause, and the bag was not walking.
A *because* clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.
*who* is already the subject of *came*, so *she* is repeated.
*Despite* takes a noun or an *-ing* form; a clause needs *although*.
The main clause is past (*I left*), so the purpose clause takes *could*.
A future time clause takes the present, not *will*.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a teacher explaining why you missed a class last week and what you did so that you would not fall behind the rest of the group.
checklist: At least one reason clause with *because*, *since* or *as*.
At least one purpose clause with *so that* or *in order to*.
No sentence uses *although* with *but*, or *because* with *so*.

topics.prompt: Some schools ban mobile phones during lessons. Give your view, and admit one argument on the other side before you close.
checklist: At least two contrast clauses with *although*, *even though* or *whereas*.
Every adverb clause is attached to a main clause, with no fragments.
A comma follows every adverb clause that comes first.

topics.prompt: Describe how your home district has changed since you were a child. Say what life was like before the change, what happened, and what people do now.
checklist: At least three time clauses with *before*, *after*, *when*, *since* or *until*.
At least one reduced clause beginning with an *-ing* form or with *having*, sharing the subject of the main clause.
Any future plan uses a present form after *when* or *after*, not *will*.
